extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film students, film scholars, filmmakers interested in genre conventions
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the characteristic elements used to recognize, analyze, or produce screwball comedy films — a subgenre of romantic comedy prominent in 1930s–1940s Hollywood. The page lists narrative, stylistic, thematic, and social-location traits with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirizes the traditional love story
rubrics_metrics.description: Screwball comedy is a film subgenre of the romantic comedy genre that satirizes the traditional love story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What sets the screwball comedy apart from the generic romantic comedy is that 'screwball comedy puts the emphasis on a funny spoofing of love, while the more traditional romantic comedy ultimately accents love.' Examples: It Happened One Night (1934), My Man Godfrey (1936).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant female / role reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguished by a female character who dominates the relationship with the male central character, whose masculinity is challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The female is often self-confident and stubborn; the masculine part usually loses the 'battle' (role reversion). Examples: Bringing Up Baby (Katharine Hepburn), The Lady Eve (Barbara Stanwyck).

rubrics_metrics.name: Battle of the sexes (verbal and physical)
rubrics_metrics.description: A humorous 'battle of the sexes' between the lead characters, including physical confrontations as well as verbal sparring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbal sparring often stands in for physical/sexual tension (especially under the Hays Code). Andrew Sarris described screwball as 'a sex comedy without the sex.' Examples: His Girl Friday (1940), You Can't Take It with You (1938).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast-paced, overlapping repartee (witty dialogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Films typically feature fast-paced, overlapping repartee and fast-talking, witty exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stylistic device is central to the genre and is a defining audio/linguistic characteristic. Examples: His Girl Friday, You Can't Take It with You; inspired later television/dialogue-driven shows (e.g., Gilmore Girls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Farcical situations and ridiculous plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes farcical, often ridiculous situations as a core element of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include absurd plot devices like caring for a pet leopard (Bringing Up Baby). Farce connects screwball films to theatrical farce and bedroom farce traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slapstick and physical comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of slapstick elements, pratfalls, and physical humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical comedy complements verbal wit; examples include Henry Fonda's pratfalls in The Lady Eve and various slapstick sequences across the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise, masquerade, and secrecy (including cross-dressing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Masquerades and disguises in which characters resort to secrecy are common, sometimes including male cross-dressing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masquerade furthers comic misunderstandings and class-passing plots. Examples: Bringing Up Baby, Love Crazy, I Was a Male War Bride, Some Like It Hot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plotlines involving courtship, marriage, and remarriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots often center on courtship, marriage, or remarriage (the 'comedy of remarriage' subgenre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarriage plots frequently show divorce and then a return to marriage, reflecting changing moral codes; examples include The Ex-Mrs. Bradford, The Awful Truth, The Philadelphia Story, His Girl Friday.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-class romantic attachments / class conflict satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic attachments frequently occur between members of different social classes, often satirizing upper-class idleness and privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common device: lower-class characters insinuate themselves into high society, showing the upper class's difficulty coping. Examples: It Happened One Night, My Man Godfrey, The Lady Eve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escapist themes with social critique (Great Depression context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Escapist themes combined with a social-class critique, arising partly from the Great Depression era context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screwball comedies gave audiences escapism while covertly addressing class tensions; studios used the format to avoid censorship by the Hays Code while still incorporating risqué elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eccentric, oddball characters / 'nutty behavior'
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters often display oddball or 'nutty' behavior used as a prism to view a topsy-turvy social moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'screwball' originally described oddball people or unpredictable movement; performers like Carole Lombard and Katharine Hepburn exemplify this eccentricity in motion and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mismatched-couple dynamic with the woman initiating the union
rubrics_metrics.description: At first the couple appears mismatched or hostile, but they amusingly overcome differences; the woman often plans the final romantic union while the man remains oblivious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dynamic is a narrative engine: the woman's agency and orchestration of events propel the plot (Bringing Up Baby quote: 'He's the man I'm going to marry. He doesn't know it, but I am.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied sexual tension handled through dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual/romantic tension is suggested rather than explicit, often handled through verbal sparring and innuendo due to Production Code constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critic Andrew Sarris's phrase 'a sex comedy without the sex' captures this; filmmakers used clever dialogue and situations to imply risqué elements covertly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical recurring settings and situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain locations and set pieces recur (e.g., Connecticut, New York City, trains) and function as genre staples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settings like Connecticut or trains enable class contrasts and mobility-driven plots; critics note geographic recurrence (Bringing Up Baby, The Palm Beach Story).
